Surat al-Infitar (The Cleaving) is Makki (revealed in Mecca), and it has nineteen verses.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

﴿When the sky is cleft asunder,﴾ ﴿and when the stars are scattered,﴾ ﴿and when the seas are burst forth,﴾ ﴿and when the graves are overturned,﴾ ﴿a soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind.﴾ ﴿O mankind, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous,﴾ ﴿who created you, then proportioned you, then made you balanced,﴾ ﴿in whatever form He willed, He assembled you?﴾ ﴿No! Rather, you deny the Recompense.﴾ ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians,﴾ [al-Infitar: 10] ﴿noble recorders,﴾ [al-Infitar: 11] ﴿who know what you do.﴾ [al-Infitar: 12] ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss,﴾ [al-Infitar: 13] ﴿and indeed, the wicked will be in the Hellfire,﴾ [al-Infitar: 14] ﴿they will burn therein on the Day of Recompense,﴾ [al-Infitar: 15] ﴿and they will not be absent from it.﴾ [al-Infitar: 16] ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 17] ﴿Then what will make you know what the Day of Recompense is?﴾ [al-Infitar: 18] ﴿The Day when no soul will have power for another soul at all, and the command that Day belongs to God.﴾ [al-Infitar: 19]

(Ba'thartu al-mata': I turned the goods over, making the back into the belly. Ba'thartu al-hawd wa-bahthartuhu: I demolished the basin and made its upper part its lower part.)

This surah is Makki, and the discussion of its cleaving (infitar) has already been given. The scattering of the stars (intithar al-kawakib) means their falling from their places, like beads of a necklace scattered when the string breaks.

The majority of readers recite (futtijarat) with a doubled jim (fujjirat). Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, al-Za'farani and al-Thawri read it with a single jim (fujarat), meaning the seas are burst forth through their being filled: they will overflow from above and spill over what is near them, or they will be emptied from below, and God will remove their water wherever He wills. It is also reported from Mujahid that he read fajarat as an active verb with a single jim, meaning "they rebelled" (baghat), because the barrier between them is removed, in light of God's words: ﴿They do not transgress against each other﴾ [al-Rahman: 20], since rebellion (baghy) and bursting forth (fajr) are opposites.

(Bu'thirat): Ibn 'Abbas said: it was searched (buhithat). al-Suddi said: it was stirred up for the resurrection of the dead. al-Farra' said: what was in its belly of gold and silver was brought out. al-Zamakhshari said: ba'thara and bahthara have the same meaning, and both are compounded of ba'th and bahth with a raa' added to them, and the meaning is: it was searched and its dead were brought out. It has been said that Bara'a (surah 9) was called al-Muba'thira, because it exposed (ba'tharat) the secrets of the hypocrites. End of his words. Rather, they are two different roots, though they agree in meaning. As for one of them being compounded from such-and-such, that is not the case. A parallel to this is the expressions: damith and dimthar, and sabit and sibatr.

﴿What it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾: the discussion of its like has already been given in the surah of al-Qiyamah (Resurrection).

The majority read ﴿mā gharraka﴾ with mā as an interrogative. Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash read ma aghraka with a hamza, which may be an exclamation (ta'ajjub), and may be an interrogative, with aghraka meaning "made you enter into gharr" (heedlessness). al-Zamakhshari said: from your saying, "gharra al-rajul fa-huwa gharr" when he was heedless, and from your saying, "bayna-hum al-'aduww wa-hum gharrun" (the enemy was among them while they were heedless), and aghharahu ghayruhu: he made him heedless. End of his words.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ and said: "His ignorance." This was also said by 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), and he recited ﴿Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. This applies to the disbeliever and to the sinner. Qatadah said: His enemy who has been empowered over him. It has been said: God's concealing (sitr) of him. It has been said: God's generosity and kindness, which teach this answer, so this is kindness to the sinful believer. It has been said: His forgiveness of him if He does not punish him the first time. al-Fudayl (may God be pleased with him) said: His lingering concealment. Ibn al-Simak said:

O one who hides sin, are you not ashamed, while God is watching you in privacy?

What has deceived you about your Lord is His respite for you, and His concealing your evil deeds for so long.

al-Zamakhshari said, in reply to al-Fudayl: this is by way of acknowledging the error of being deceived by the concealment, not by way of an excuse as the greedy man supposes, and as the storytellers of the Hashwiyya suppose, and as they narrate from their imams. He only said ﴿the Generous﴾ rather than any of His other attributes, so that He would teach His servant the answer, until he says: "What deceived me was His being the Generous." End of his words. This is his habit in criticizing the people of the Sunnah.

﴿Proportioned you﴾ (sawwaka): He made you sound in your limbs. ﴿Made you balanced﴾ (fa'adalaka): He made you upright and proportionate in creation, without disparity.

(p. 437) al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Talhah, al-A'mash, 'Isa, Abu Ja'far and the Kufans read ﴿fa'adalaka﴾ with a light dal (fa-'adalaka), while the rest of the Seven read it with a doubled dal (fa'addalaka). The light reading may be like the doubled reading, meaning He balanced some of your limbs with others until they became balanced; or its meaning may be "He turned you," as in "'adalahu 'an al-tariq," meaning "He turned him aside from the road": He turned you away from the creation of others to a beautiful creation distinct from the rest of creation, or He made you into some of the forms and appearances. The apparent sense is that His saying ﴿in whatever form﴾ is connected to ﴿your Lord﴾, meaning He placed you in a form that His will required, of beauty, height, maleness, resemblance to some relatives, or the opposite of that. "Ma" is extra, and "shā'a" is in the position of a qualifier for "ṣūra" (form). He did not connect ﴿rakkabaka﴾ with fa- as in the preceding clause, because it is an explanation of ﴿fa'adalaka﴾. That ﴿fī ayyi ṣūratin﴾ is connected to ﴿rabbika﴾ is the view of the majority. It has been said that it is connected to a deleted element, meaning: He assembled you in some of the forms. Some of the interpreters said that it is connected to His saying ﴿fa'adalaka﴾, meaning: He balanced you in a form, whatever form, and ayy indicates wonder and magnification, so He did not make you in the form of a pig or a donkey. On this view, ma is in the accusative governed by "shā'a," as if He said: "in whatever fine assembly He willed, He assembled you." Tarkib (assembly) means putting together and joining one thing to another.

Kharijah, on the authority of Nafi', assimilated ﴿rakkabaka kalla﴾ (rakkabakk kallā), as Abu 'Amr did in his major assimilation (idgham al-kabir).

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rebuke and a deterrent against what the preceding clause indicates of their being deceived about God, or against what the clause after kalla indicates of their denial of the Day of Recompense and religion, or the law of Islam.

The majority read ﴿tukadhdhibūna﴾ (you deny) with ta', as address to the disbelievers, while al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Abu Bishr read it with ya' (yukadhdhibūna), in the third person.

This surah is Makki, and the discussion of its cleaving (infitar) has already been given. The scattering of the stars (intithar al-kawakib) means their falling from their places, like beads of a necklace scattered when the string breaks.

The majority of readers recite (futtijarat) with a doubled jim (fujjirat). Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, al-Za'farani and al-Thawri read it with a single jim (fujarat), meaning the seas are burst forth through their being filled: they will overflow from above and spill over what is near them, or they will be emptied from below, and God will remove their water wherever He wills. It is also reported from Mujahid that he read fajarat as an active verb with a single jim, meaning "they rebelled" (baghat), because the barrier between them is removed, in light of God's words: ﴿They do not transgress against each other﴾ [al-Rahman: 20], since rebellion (baghy) and bursting forth (fajr) are opposites.

(Bu'thirat): Ibn 'Abbas said: it was searched (buhithat). al-Suddi said: it was stirred up for the resurrection of the dead. al-Farra' said: what was in its belly of gold and silver was brought out. al-Zamakhshari said: ba'thara and bahthara have the same meaning, and both are compounded of ba'th and bahth with a raa' added to them, and the meaning is: it was searched and its dead were brought out. It has been said that Bara'a (surah 9) was called al-Muba'thira, because it exposed (ba'tharat) the secrets of the hypocrites. End of his words. The apparent sense of his statement that both are compounded is that their root is what has been mentioned, and that the raa' was added to this root; but the matter is not as his words imply, because the raa' is not one of the letters of augmentation. Rather, they are two different roots, though they agree in meaning. As for one of them being compounded from such-and-such, that is not the case. A parallel to this is the expressions: damith and dimthar, and sabit and sibatr.

﴿What it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾: the discussion of its like has already been given in the surah of al-Qiyamah (Resurrection).

The majority read ﴿mā gharraka﴾ with mā as an interrogative. Ibn Jubayr and al-A'mash read ma aghraka with a hamza, which may be an exclamation (ta'ajjub), and may be an interrogative, with aghraka meaning "made you enter into gharr" (heedlessness). al-Zamakhshari said: from your saying, "gharra al-rajul fa-huwa gharr" when he was heedless, and from your saying, "bayna-hum al-'aduww wa-hum gharrun" (the enemy was among them while they were heedless), and aghharahu ghayruhu: he made him heedless. End of his words.

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ and said: "His ignorance." This was also said by 'Umar (may God be pleased with him), and he recited ﴿Indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab: 72]. This applies to the disbeliever and to the sinner. Qatadah said: His enemy who has been empowered over him. It has been said: God's concealing (sitr) of him. It has been said: God's generosity and kindness, which teach this answer, so this is kindness to the sinful believer. It has been said: His forgiveness of him if He does not punish him the first time. al-Fudayl (may God be pleased with him) said: His lingering concealment. Ibn al-Simak said:

O one who hides sin, are you not ashamed, while God is watching you in privacy?

What has deceived you about your Lord is His respite for you, and His concealing your evil deeds for so long.

al-Zamakhshari said, in reply to al-Fudayl: this is by way of acknowledging the error of being deceived by the concealment, not by way of an excuse as the greedy man supposes, and as the storytellers of the Hashwiyya suppose, and as they narrate from their imams. He only said ﴿the Generous﴾ rather than any of His other attributes, so that He would teach His servant the answer, until he says: "What deceived me was His being the Generous." End of his words. This is his habit in criticizing the people of the Sunnah.

﴿Proportioned you﴾ (sawwaka): He made you sound in your limbs. ﴿Made you balanced﴾ (fa'adalaka): He made you upright and proportionate in creation, without disparity.

(p. 437) al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Talhah, al-A'mash, 'Isa, Abu Ja'far and the Kufans read ﴿fa'adalaka﴾ with a light dal (fa-'adalaka), while the rest of the Seven read it with a doubled dal (fa'addalaka). The light reading may be like the doubled reading, meaning He balanced some of your limbs with others until they became balanced; or its meaning may be "He turned you," as in "'adalahu 'an al-tariq," meaning "He turned him aside from the road": He turned you away from the creation of others to a beautiful creation distinct from the rest of creation, or He made you into some of the forms and appearances. The apparent sense is that His saying ﴿in whatever form﴾ is connected to ﴿your Lord﴾, meaning He placed you in a form that His will required, of beauty, height, maleness, resemblance to some relatives, or the opposite of that. "Ma" is extra, and "shā'a" is in the position of a qualifier for "ṣūra" (form). He did not connect ﴿rakkabaka﴾ with fa- as in the preceding clause, because it is an explanation of ﴿fa'adalaka﴾. That ﴿fī ayyi ṣūratin﴾ is connected to ﴿rabbika﴾ is the view of the majority. It has been said that it is connected to a deleted element, meaning: He assembled you in some of the forms. Some of the interpreters said that it is connected to His saying ﴿fa'adalaka﴾, meaning: He balanced you in a form, whatever form, and ayy indicates wonder and magnification, so He did not make you in the form of a pig or a donkey. On this view, ma is in the accusative governed by "shā'a," as if He said: "in whatever fine assembly He willed, He assembled you." Tarkib (assembly) means putting together and joining one thing to another.

Kharijah, on the authority of Nafi', assimilated ﴿rakkabaka kalla﴾ (rakkabakk kallā), as Abu 'Amr did in his major assimilation (idgham al-kabir).

﴿Kalla﴾ (No!) is a rebuke and a deterrent against what the preceding clause indicates of their being deceived about God, or against what the clause after kalla indicates of their denial of the Day of Recompense and religion, or the law of Islam.

The majority read ﴿tukadhdhibūna﴾ (you deny) with ta', as address to the disbelievers, while al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Shaybah and Abu Bishr read it with ya' (yukadhdhibūna), in the third person.

﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh piece of information). That is, over them are those who preserve their deeds and record them. It appears that it is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), and the *wāw* is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-hāl*), meaning: "you who deny the Day of Recompense." "Al-Kātibūn" are the guardians (*al-hafazah*) who record your deeds so that you may be recompensed for them. In praising the scribes, there is an exaltation of the matter of recompense.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of reciters) read *yaslawnahā* as the imperfect of *ṣaliya*, in its light form (*mukhaffafan*). Ibn Miqsam read it in the intensive form (*mushaddadan*), in the passive voice (*mabniyyan lil-maf'ūl*). ﴿They know what you do﴾: so they record what the recompense is attached to. Al-Hasan said: "They know what is apparent, not the inner talk of the soul (*ḥadīth al-nafs*)." Sufyan said: "When the servant intends a good deed or an evil deed, the two scribes perceive its scent." Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: "Since He said *ya'lamūn* (they know) and did not say *yaktubūn* (they write), this indicates that they do not write down everything; thus excluded are forgetfulness, error, and what carries no consequence." ﴿And they will not be absent from it﴾: that is, from the Hellfire; that is, they cannot be absent from it, like His saying: ﴿And they will not be brought out of the Fire﴾ [al-Baqarah: 167]. It was also said: they are witnessing it in the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm), and since He informed about their being crucified (*ṣalb*) on the Day of Resurrection, He informed about the negation of their absence from it before the burning (*ṣalī*), that is, they see their places in the Fire.

﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgement is?﴾ is an exaltation of the terror of that Day. Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿĪsā, Ibn Jundub, Ibn Kathir, and Abu ʿAmr read *yawmu lā tamliku* with a *ḍamma* on the *mīm* (*yawmu*), meaning: it is a day. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be a substitute (*badal*) for what precedes it. Maḥbūb, from Abu ʿAmr, read *yawmun lā tamliku* indefinite, with *tanwīn* and in the nominative, detaching it from the construct (*fakkahu ʿani l-idāfah*); its nominative status is based on "it is a day." *Lā tamliku* is a clause in the place of a qualifier (*ṣifah*), and the returning pronoun (*al-ʿāʾid*) is omitted, meaning: *lā tamliku fīhi* (no soul will have power in it). Zayd ibn ʿAlī, al-Hasan, Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj, and the rest of the seven read *yawma* with a *fatḥa*, as an adverb of time (*ẓarf*). According to the Basrans, this is a case-ending vowel (*ḥarakat iʿrāb*, the vowel that marks grammatical case), and according to the Kufans it may be a built-form vowel (*ḥarakat binā'*, a fixed vowel not governed by case). On both views it is in the place of a nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "the recompense is on the day when no soul will have power"; or in the place of an accusative as an adverb, meaning: "they will be recompensed on the day when no soul will have power"; or as an object, meaning: "remember the day when no soul will have power." On the view of one who permits its being built, it may be in the place of a nominative as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "it is (the day) when no soul will have power" ﴿for any soul over another soul in anything﴾, which is general, like His saying: ﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm another﴾ [Saba': 42]. Muqatil said: "for a disbelieving soul, anything of benefit."

﴿And the command on that Day belongs to Allah﴾. Qatadah said: "Likewise it is the Day (of which it is said that the command belongs to Allah) in this world as well, but there no one claims any dispute, and He does not permit anyone to retain what he possessed in this world."
